sources.title: ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group: Nonconformity - review and closing (Edition 1, 13 January 2016)
supportedClaims: An organization's response to a nonconformity has three parts: correction, analysis of cause and corrective action.

ISO 9000 defines nonconformity as non-fulfillment of a requirement, correction as action to eliminate a detected nonconformity, and corrective action as action to eliminate the cause of a nonconformity and to prevent recurrence.
Corrective action cannot be taken without first determining the cause; methods range from brainstorming to root cause analysis, fish-bone diagrams and 5 Whys.
The first failure factor found should not be assumed to be the root cause; factors are categorized as not able to confirm, possible or confirmed, and the analysis and conclusions are recorded.
Organizations should check whether a cause was systematic or accidental; treating a systematic failure as a one-off means corrective action will not succeed.

Auditors verify clear statements of actions, thorough descriptions referencing specific documents, past tense, completion dates and evidence that corrective action was implemented as described and did not create further problems.

Correction or corrective action alone can be sufficient in some cases, and the need for comprehensive root cause analysis depends on the nature of the finding and whether it suggests a systemic failure.

Before closing, a nonconformity needs objective evidence that the corrective action is fully implemented and effective at preventing recurrence; closure may be by on-site examination or remote review of documentary evidence.
Cause analysis can reveal potential nonconformities elsewhere in the organization and informs risk-based planning.
The paper was written for ISO 9001:2015 and is auditor guidance that has not been endorsed by ISO, TC 176 or IAF; it does not establish current edition requirements.

sources.title: ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group: Nonconformity - Documenting (13 January 2016)
supportedClaims: A well-documented nonconformity has three parts: the audit evidence, the requirement and the statement of nonconformity.
Requirements can come from the standard, the organization's own management system, regulations or the customer.
The statement of nonconformity drives cause analysis, correction and corrective action, so it should be precise, unambiguous and not a restatement of the evidence.
Systematic recording, for example on a Nonconformity Report form, gives traceability, progress review and evidence of completion and effectiveness of corrective actions.

The example NCR form separates details, root cause analysis, correction with dates, corrective action with dates, review of the plan, verification of implementation, verification of effectiveness and close-out.

sources.title: NIST Radiation Physics Division Quality Management System Guide RPD-G-08 Corrective Action (version 2.11)
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
supportedClaims: One NIST laboratory's procedure has the responsible party investigate the root cause and record it on a Corrective Action Plan form.
Corrective actions are selected to fit the root cause, eliminate the problem and prevent recurrence, and the group leader reviews and signs the plan.
Affected organizations are notified and required changes are documented and implemented.
Results are monitored after completion to confirm the desired effect, with monitoring appropriate to the nature of the action.
Where doubt is cast on compliance with the quality system, the affected areas are audited.
Acceptance requires demonstrating quality is restored before regular service resumes, and the investigator, group leader, quality manager and division chief sign the plan.
The quality manager files the original plan.
This is one laboratory's process for calibration and testing services, not ISO 9001 guidance.

sources.title: NIST Radiation Physics Division Quality Management System Guide RPD-G-07 Nonconformance (version 2.11)
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
supportedClaims: Nonconforming work may be identified through internal or external audits, management reviews, the process itself, client feedback or staff observation, and complaints may reveal it.
Personnel first identify whether the work is truly nonconforming, then evaluate its significance and determine root cause through the corrective action procedure.

Different situations follow different routes: some require only notifying the client and documenting, equipment malfunction stops work and proceeds to corrective action, and a need to revise procedures proceeds to corrective action.
If a client chooses to accept nonconforming work, the acceptance must be in writing and placed in the client's file.
Not every nonconformance requires the corrective action form.
This is one laboratory's process, not ISO 9001 guidance.
